title: Enuma Elish, Tablet V: the ordering of the universe
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.2, Poem of Creation (Enuma elish) (ed. A. C. Heinrich, rev. Z. J. Földi and E. Jiménez), SB V) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Enuma Elish (the Babylonian Poem of Creation), Tablet V: 135 of 158 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (5 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
Marduk sets the stars, the year and the moon in their courses, forms features of the world from Tiamat's body, returns to the gods, is acclaimed king, and announces the building of Babylon.

Enuma Elish ('When on high'), the Babylonian Poem of Creation, tells how Marduk, god of Babylon, defeated Tiamat, created the ordered world and became king of the gods. It was written on seven tablets and recited in Babylon during the New Year festival. The date of composition is debated (proposals range from the 18th to the 12th century BCE); the surviving copies date from the 9th to the 2nd century BCE and come from Ashur, Nineveh, Kish, Babylon, Sippar, Uruk and other sites. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/V) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so (BM.38049, BM.43969). The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 135 of the 158 lines of the eBL edition (85%), from 5 tablets in the British Museum: K.3567 (Nineveh), K.3445 (Nineveh), BM.38049, 1879,0708.47 (Nineveh), BM.43969.

Lines not shown. 23 of the 158 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 64 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara); commentary: BM.66606); 65-69 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara)); 70 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara); commentary: Rm.395, BM.66606); 71-76 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara)); 81-82 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara); quotation in another text: 79.B.1/30, BM.38706); 83 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara); commentary: BM.66606; quotation in another text: BM.32206); 84 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara); commentary: BM.66606); 85-89 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara)); 90 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.98 (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara), VAT.12915 (Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin); commentary: Rm.395). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; : divider sign written on the tablet; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet; (gloss: ...) a note written by the scribe in small signs or in the margin.

translation.text:
1He made positions for the great gods,
2He set up constellations, the star images.
3He marked the year, drew (its) boundaries,
4He set up twelve months of three stars each.
5After he had laid out the plan for the days of the year,
6He fixed the position of Neberu to mark the (stars’) relationships.
7Lest any make an error or go astray,
8He established the position(s) of Enlil and Ea in relation to it.
9He opened up gates on both (sides of her) ribs,
10He made strong bolts to left and right.
11He established the heights in her vitals,
12He made the moon appear, entrusted (to him) the night.
13He assigned to him the crown jewel of nighttime to mark the days (of the month),
14Every month, without ceasing, he exalted him with a crown.
15“At the beginning of the month, waxing over the land,
16“You shine with two horns to mark the naming of six days,
17“At the seventh day, the crown is [ha]lf.
18“At the fifteenth day, you shall be in opposition, at the midpoint of each [month].
19“When the sun can see you on the horizon,
20“Wane at the same pace and form in reverse.
21“At the day of di[sappeara]nce, approach the sun's course,
22“On the thirtieth day, you shall be in conjunction with the sun as a double.
23“I d[efined?] the celestial signs, proceed on their path,
24“[…] approach each other and render (oracular) judgment.
25“You, the sun, … shall abjure murder, wrong-doing,
26“[…] me.”
translation.scan_note: British Museum K.3567: obverse, the tablet's own lines 1 to 26. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/V) attributes SB V 1-26 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges, ink K.3567 on the bottom edge and K.8588 on a joined piece. About 25 to 27 lines on the obverse and exactly two lines on the otherwise blank reverse, matching eBL's 27 obverse lines of Tablet V and one reverse line each of Tablets V and VI. On this tablet of line 25 only one to three signs survive and lines 1-24, 26 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.

131When the gods his fathers heard what he commanded,
132They … […]
133“Over all things that your hands have created,
134“Who has [authority, save for you]?
135“Over the earth that you have created,
136“Who has [authority, save for] you?

138“Make our [stopping place] there forever.
139“Let them bring us our daily portions,
140“[…] our […].
141“Whosoever shall […] our tasks that we […],
142“In this place […] his toil [he shall rest from].”
143They rejoiced […]
144The gods […] … them.
145He who knew […] granted him a weapon,
146He made ready to speak, enlightened them,
147… […] his command now,
148He … […] … the rituals
149[…] them […]
150And […] …
151The gods prostrated before him, saying,
152To Lugaldimmeran[ki]a, their lord, they [said],
153“Formerly, O Lord, you were our beloved son,
154“Now you are our King […]
155“He whose glory saved [our lives],
156“[… gl]ory, ma[ce] and sce[pter],
157“Let him make plans, everything demanding skill,
158“We shall [gladly execute them].”
